hints: Number the longest carbon chain containing the $C=C$ to give the double bond the lowest possible locant, then check where the double bond starts for A.
For B and C, confirm both have the same connectivity $CH_3CH=CHCH_3$ and differ only in spatial arrangement around the restricted $C=C$.
Compare the positions of the two $CH_3$ groups in B versus C to decide which has both bulky groups on the same side (cis, Z) and which has them on opposite sides (trans, E).
For D, identify the longest chain through the $C=C$ and count the methyl substituent on the double bonded carbon to build the branched systematic name.
walkthrough:
Name the straight chain terminal alkene A**
Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. You have four carbons in a row with the double bond starting at carbon 1 if you number from the right. That gives but-1-ene. The 1 is essential because but-2-ene would be a different position.

Spot that B and C are the same connectivity**
Both B and C show $\text{CH}_3$ on each carbon of the $C=C$. So both are but-2-ene. The $C=C$ cannot rotate, so the two different spatial arrangements are locked as separate stereoisomers.

Assign cis and trans using the diagrams**
In B both $\text{H}$ atoms are drawn on top and both $\text{CH}_3$ groups below the $C=C$. Same side means cis, so B is cis-but-2-ene, also called (Z)-but-2-ene. In C one $\text{CH}_3$ is top left and the other $\text{CH}_3$ is bottom right, so they are on opposite sides. That is trans, so C is trans-but-2-ene, also called (E)-but-2-ene.

Name the branched alkene D**
$\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ has three carbons in the longest chain through the double bond, with a methyl branch on carbon 2. Numbering to give the double bond locant 1 gives 2-methylprop-1-ene, often shortened to methylpropene.

Final answer: A: but-1-ene
B: cis-but-2-ene / (Z)-but-2-ene
C: trans-but-2-ene / (E)-but-2-ene
D: 2-methylprop-1-ene / methylpropene

hints: Think what stays the same (connectivity, structural formula) and what changes (3D arrangement in space) for stereoisomers like B and C.
walkthrough:
Separate connectivity from geometry**
Picture B and C side by side. The atoms are joined in exactly the same order, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. Nothing about which atom bonds to which has changed. What is different is purely how the groups point in space around the rigid $C=C$, same side versus opposite sides. That is the heart of stereoisomerism: same structural formula, different spatial arrangement.
Final answer: Compounds with the same structural formula but with a different arrangement of atoms or groups in space.

hints: Add $H^+$ to each end of the $C=C$ in turn and see which alkene A, B, C or D can give both $CH_3C^+(H)(CH_2CH_3)$ and $H_2C^+CH_2CH_2CH_3$.
walkthrough:
Match the carbocations to the parent alkene**
Take $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. If $H^+$ adds to the terminal $\text{CH}_2$, the positive charge lands on carbon 2 to give $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{(H)(CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)}$. If $H^+$ adds to the internal $\text{CH}$, the charge lands on carbon 1 to give $\text{H}_2\text{C}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Only the unsymmetrical terminal alkene A can give this primary plus secondary pair. B, C and D would give different carbocations.

hints: Recall that $HBr$ adds so $Br^-$ attacks the more stable carbocation, forming 2-bromobutane $CH_3CHBrCH_2CH_3$ as the major product.
Compare the two possible intermediates, a secondary carbocation versus a primary carbocation, and decide which is lower in energy.
Link stability to electron donation by alkyl groups, considering how many alkyl groups surround the positively charged carbon in each case.
walkthrough:
Draw the major product skeleton**
$H^+$ adds first, then $Br^-$ bonds to the carbocation carbon. Attack on the secondary carbocation puts $Br$ on carbon 2. So you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. In skeletal form draw a four carbon zigzag and attach $Br$ to the second vertex from the left. That is 2-bromobutane.

Choose the lower energy pathway**
Think of the $C^+$ as electron deficient and hungry for electron density. The secondary ion $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{(H)(CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)}$ has two carbon groups pushing electron density toward it, while the primary ion $\text{H}_2\text{C}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ has only one. More donation means more stabilised charge, so the secondary carbocation forms faster and in greater amount.

Explain the stabilisation with the inductive effect**
Alkyl groups are electron releasing by the positive inductive effect. With two alkyl groups, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, donating to the $C^+$, the secondary carbocation spreads and reduces the concentrated positive charge much more effectively than the single alkyl group in the primary ion. That is why the route via the secondary ion dominates and 2-bromobutane is the major product, a classic Markovnikov outcome.

Final answer: Major product is 2-bromobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, drawn as skeletal formula with Br on the second carbon.
Formed via the more stable secondary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{(H)(CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)}$.
This carbocation is more stable due to greater positive inductive electron donation from two alkyl groups compared to one alkyl group in the primary carbocation.

hints: Compare formulas $CH_3CH_2CH_2OH$ and $CH_3CH=CH_2$ to see what small molecule is lost when the alkene forms.
walkthrough:
Track the atoms lost**
Go from propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, to propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$. You have lost $H$ and $OH$, in other words $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. A reagent that removes water in this way is acting as a dehydrating agent.
Final answer: Dehydrating agent (causes dehydration / removal of water).

hints: Recall what type of change acidified $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$ brings about when an alcohol is converted to a carbonyl compound.
walkthrough:
Recognise the oxidising system**
Warm acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is the classic oxidiser that turns an alcohol $Y$ into a carbonyl $Z$ by removing hydrogen or adding oxygen. So $Y$ to $Z$ is oxidation.

hints: Remember which carbonyl functional group alone gives a silver mirror with Tollens reagent, and why distillation helps isolate it.
walkthrough:
Use the silver mirror clue**
Only aldehydes are oxidised easily enough by Tollens reagent to deposit metallic silver as a mirror. Ketones do not react, and a carboxylic acid would mean over oxidation had occurred. Because $Z$ is distilled off immediately, it is stopped at the aldehyde stage before it can be oxidised further to the acid. So tick aldehyde only.
Final answer: aldehyde ticked only (ketone blank, carboxylic acid blank)
